r00.text: CREATE TABLE names the table. Inside the parentheses, each line names a column and its type, followed by any rules. NOT NULL requires a value for the name. Without it, SQL can represent a missing name with NULL, a marker for absence rather than the text “NULL” or an empty string. Missing values need care in comparisons and totals; Values, missing data and equality [/review/relational-collection/values/] develops those rules.

Separating facts this way is part of data modelling: deciding what one row means, which values identify it and which facts belong with it. Normalisation is the discipline of using those dependencies to avoid storing the same fact in several places where the copies can disagree. Relations, keys and normalisation [/review/relational-collection/modelling/] works through those choices, including when a deliberate copy is useful.

This query reads the inputs and produces a result; it does not store the receipt as a new table or change the existing rows. The drawing filters first to make the matching easy to follow. An actual database can use a different route to produce the same answer, perhaps looking up the relevant lines through an index. Understanding the result and understanding the work it takes are separate questions. Query execution and bad plans [/review/relational-collection/query-execution/] follows the latter.

An ordinary JOIN, also called an inner join, keeps only matches. A left join can retain an order even when the payment side has no matching row, filling that side with NULL. That is how order 103 can remain visible in a report of unpaid orders. Joins and the meaning of a result row [/review/relational-collection/query-results/] builds this report without losing unpaid orders or multiplying their amounts; Aggregates, windows and ordered results [/review/relational-collection/aggregates-and-windows/] develops the calculations.

Constraints and tenant boundaries [/review/relational-collection/constraints/] explains which rules can be enforced directly and how to express them. The first design question is which states must be impossible, then which combination of constraints and transaction logic makes them impossible.

Acknowledging a commit also carries a promise about crashes. With PostgreSQL’s normal durability settings and storage that honours flush requests, a successful commit survives a database crash. PostgreSQL records changes in a write-ahead log on durable storage; after a crash it can replay that log to recover changes whose table pages were still in memory. Write-ahead logs and crash recovery [/review/relational-collection/crash-recovery/] follows the writes and the settings that change this promise.

That promise has a boundary. A database transaction does not reach into a card provider and roll its charge back, or pull back an email that has been sent. Work across those boundaries needs its own protocol. Outboxes and database-backed jobs [/review/relational-collection/outboxes-and-jobs/] shows how to commit a record of work alongside the change that requires it.

Nor does a dropped connection tell the application whether a commit succeeded. The server may have committed just before the reply was lost. Sending the purchase again could create a duplicate unless the application can recognise the same request. Retries when a commit reply is missing [/review/relational-collection/conflicts-and-retries/] develops that case. It is a different uncertainty from a transaction known to have rolled back.

This is the division of work to remember. Constraints reject forbidden data states. Atomicity groups the changes that belong together. Isolation, locks and correctly written updates govern how transactions interact. They help you implement a business rule; they need a business rule and a transaction design to implement. Transactions and isolation [/review/relational-collection/transaction-boundaries/] continues from this purchase, and Locks, contention and deadlocks [/review/relational-collection/locks-and-deadlocks/] follows what waiting costs.

For a next step, choose the question you now want to answer. If it is how to turn your application’s facts into tables, continue with Relations, keys and normalisation [/review/relational-collection/modelling/]. If it is how to assemble an answer, follow Joins and the meaning of a result row [/review/relational-collection/query-results/]. If it is how two writers can change shared data safely, start Transactions and isolation [/review/relational-collection/transaction-boundaries/].

Once the answers are correct, Indexes and access paths [/review/relational-collection/indexes/] explains how an index can find a few matching rows without reading the whole table, and what that extra structure costs each write. SQL at the application boundary [/review/relational-collection/application-sql/] takes the queries into application code. Before depending on the data, work through Backup, restore and reconciliation [/review/relational-collection/backup-and-restore/]; a database can faithfully preserve a mistaken change too. Replicas, lag and read routing [/review/relational-collection/replicas-and-read-routing/] then follows what a second copy adds, and why it may answer with older data.

r01.text: Removing order 102 reveals a deletion anomaly. Removing the only sale carrying Tariq’s details also removes the fact that he is a customer. With separate tables, deleting an order and deleting a customer are distinct decisions. Whether the shop should retain either is a lifecycle policy; History, correction and deletion [/review/relational-collection/data-lifecycle/] develops that policy.

Normalisation gives a rule a suitable home; the SQL declarations and write protocol enforce it. An order_items table without the declared composite key could still admit duplicate line identities. A customers table without its key could make the reconstruction multiply lines. Constraints and tenant boundaries [/review/relational-collection/constraints/] follows the enforcement, including references that must remain inside one shop.

That is deliberate denormalisation: accepting redundant storage for a defined use while owning the risk of disagreement. A vague expectation that application code will “keep it in sync” leaves the original anomaly intact. First establish the correct model, then use query measurements to decide which copy earns its upkeep. Query execution and bad plans [/review/relational-collection/query-execution/] helps identify the work before changing the design.

r02.text: Choose the rule for the field’s job. A person’s name should retain their spelling; an opaque external identifier should retain the external system’s identity rules. Trimming, lowercasing or removing accents everywhere can merge values that were meant to remain distinct. Constraints and tenant boundaries [/review/relational-collection/constraints/] develops how to enforce the identity rule once you have chosen it.

Lists have the same trap. 7 NOT IN (3, NULL) is unknown: 7 differs from 3, but SQL cannot establish that it differs from the missing value. A nullable result on the right of NOT IN can therefore remove rows unexpectedly. For “no matching row exists”, use a query shaped around existence; Joins and the meaning of a result row [/review/relational-collection/query-results/] develops NOT EXISTS and the matching condition it needs.

This is different from storing a payment whose amount is unknown. An unknown amount must not quietly become a zero payment. The shop requires every payment amount, and Aggregates, windows and ordered results [/review/relational-collection/aggregates-and-windows/] follows how missing inputs affect counts, sums and averages.

r03.text: As Values, missing data and equality [/review/relational-collection/values/] showed, a PostgreSQL check rejects false and accepts true or unknown. A missing quantity makes quantity > 0 unknown, so the check alone would allow it. The two declarations work together.

UNIQUE can preserve another identity beside the primary key. If a variant introduces a generated line_id, it still needs UNIQUE (order_id, line_no) and required values for that business identity. Generating different IDs for two inserts does not stop them recording the same line twice. Relations, keys and normalisation [/review/relational-collection/modelling/] develops the choice of keys; constraints carry that choice into every write.

References also need a practical access path. PostgreSQL creates an index for a primary or unique key, but does not automatically create one on the child’s foreign-key columns. Deleting a product requires finding its lines. On a large line table an index on product_id can make that search cheaper; the line primary key already starts with order_id for the order-side search. Indexes and access paths [/review/relational-collection/indexes/] develops that cost.

Keeping those questions distinct makes testing clearer. Try a shop 10 line with a parent from another shop to test integrity. Try a well-formed shop 20 operation through a shop 10 caller to test authority. The latter should fail even though the data would be internally consistent. Database access and least privilege [/review/relational-collection/access-control/] develops runtime authority; PostgreSQL roles, policies and privileged code [/review/relational-collection/postgresql/access-control/] works through policy tests.

Such a rule needs a complete write protocol: which changes belong in one transaction, how competing writers coordinate, what each reads after waiting and which failures require a complete retry. The introduction’s conditional stock update is one protocol for one stock row; it is not a general solution to counting bookings. Transactions and isolation [/review/relational-collection/transaction-boundaries/] develops these concurrent multi-row rules.

r04.text: Then follow copies outside those declared references. A cache may outlive the row; a search document may remain searchable; an export may already be elsewhere. Record the required downstream work durably with the deletion, give that work a stable identity and check its completion. Outboxes and database-backed jobs [/review/relational-collection/outboxes-and-jobs/] develops the delivery protocol.

Backups and replicas need different treatment. A replica can carry a deletion onward, but an older backup preserves an earlier state by design. A restore can therefore reintroduce data previously removed. Keep whatever suppression or reconciliation record the restoration process needs outside the state being rolled back, and apply the chosen policy before the restored system becomes authoritative. Backup, restore and reconciliation [/review/relational-collection/backup-and-restore/] owns that recovery procedure.

r05.text: The CTEs make the reasoning readable. They do not require PostgreSQL to execute the clauses as a series of stored temporary tables. The planner may combine work while preserving the result. Query execution and bad plans [/review/relational-collection/query-execution/] follows the physical choices; Aggregates, windows and ordered results [/review/relational-collection/aggregates-and-windows/] develops the grouped calculations.

NOT IN needs more care. If its right-hand result contains a NULL, an otherwise unmatched value can produce unknown rather than true. The shop’s payments.order_id is non-missing, but a later union or optional relation could change that guarantee. NOT EXISTS keeps “no matching row” explicit; Values, missing data and equality [/review/relational-collection/values/] follows the three-valued comparisons.

r06.text: Every core order has lines, so all three appear. This definition deliberately contains orders whose value can be calculated from their lines; an order without lines would be absent. Decide how to expose incomplete orders in a production report. The earlier join article [/review/relational-collection/query-results/] keeps them visible with a missing total instead of silently calling them zero.

A condition that applies to one measure can go inside the aggregate with FILTER. On the orders table, COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE status = 'pending') counts pending orders while COUNT(*) still counts every order. Filtering the entire query to pending orders would change both measures. For a day-based report, also choose the time zone and boundaries before filtering; Values, missing data and equality [/review/relational-collection/values/] shows why a calendar day is more than a timestamp cast.

The same care applies when returning only the first few rows. A total order makes their selection deterministic within one view of the data; it does not freeze that view while another transaction changes it. Pagination and consistent exports [/review/relational-collection/large-results/] follows the order across requests.

r07.text: The shop list can use an index on (placed_at, order_id). A list restricted to one customer may instead benefit from (customer_id, placed_at, order_id), putting the fixed equality first. Other filters can force the scan to inspect and reject many entries before it finds a full page. Joins, sorting, row visibility and the cost of returned columns still matter. Indexes and access paths [/review/relational-collection/indexes/] develops that match, and Query execution and bad plans [/review/relational-collection/query-execution/] checks the work with EXPLAIN.

The fixed view still includes 103, because it qualified before the writer’s commit. The writer is free to commit; the report’s view remains older. This is the snapshot promise developed in Transactions and isolation [/review/relational-collection/transaction-boundaries/], applied to an entire result rather than a repeated stock read.

Do not leave this transaction open while a person decides whether to click “next”. For a bounded export, read promptly into an output file or other controlled destination, close the transaction, then let the user download that finished result. Limit duration, batch size and concurrency, and handle cancellation by closing the cursor and ending the transaction. Connections, overload and capacity [/review/relational-collection/connections-and-capacity/] follows the resource budgets.

r08.text: This is different from reading stock, subtracting in the application and writing the saved answer. stock = stock - 1 derives the change from the row being updated. At PostgreSQL Read Committed, a competing updater waits and then rechecks the condition against the committed replacement row. The complete purchase and other isolation levels are developed in Transactions and isolation [/review/relational-collection/transaction-boundaries/].

PostgreSQL’s Repeatable Read instead keeps the view established by the transaction’s first snapshot-taking query. Waiting for the guard does not replace that older view. The worksheet therefore requires Read Committed and requires every feed writer to follow the same guard protocol. Transactions and isolation [/review/relational-collection/transaction-boundaries/] develops the broader choice of views and write protection.

Once the data is committed, a search index, cache or external catalogue may still need updating. That work does not become atomic because the import used COPY. Record any required follow-up in the same database transaction and deliver it with its own retry protocol, as Outboxes and database-backed jobs [/review/relational-collection/outboxes-and-jobs/] develops. Live schema backfills have a different coexistence problem, covered in Live schema changes and backfills [/review/relational-collection/schema-changes/].

r09.text: fetchall() is convenient for the small lists here. It is also a promise to bring the whole remaining result into application memory. Exports need bounded reading and a defined view of changing data; Pagination and consistent exports [/review/relational-collection/large-results/] develops that contract.

Rewind to before order 103 for the purchase fragment. The mug has stock 1. The conditional update from Transactions and isolation [/review/relational-collection/transaction-boundaries/] can return one row, or none. Both are successful SQL execution. Only the first means that this attempt reserved stock.

A check violation such as 23514 usually requires fixing the input or the operation. A serialization failure, 40001, requires rerunning the complete transaction and its decisions. A transport failure during commit can leave the outcome uncertain. These are different instructions, not one generic “retry database error” branch. Retries when a commit reply is missing [/review/relational-collection/conflicts-and-retries/] handles that last distinction.

Fetching everything in one join changes a different thing: the result has one row per line, so order columns repeat. Preserve the row meaning when reconstructing objects and paginating the orders. A query count alone does not establish that the new result is correct. Inspect the generated SQL, its parameters and its transaction boundary, then measure the work for a representative request. Joins and the meaning of a result row [/review/relational-collection/query-results/] supplies the needed result reasoning.

r10.text: The planner chooses among these routes before running the query. It uses statistics to estimate how many rows will match and a cost model to compare the work. An unused index can therefore mean the planner has sensibly chosen a scan. It can also mean the estimate is wrong. Query execution and bad plans [/review/relational-collection/query-execution/] follows how to tell those cases apart.

B-trees are not the right structure for every operator. Words inside documents, array membership, spatial overlap and nearest-neighbour searches need other methods. PostgreSQL index methods and operators [/review/relational-collection/postgresql/indexes/] matches those questions to their structures. Choosing the method begins with what comparison the query asks the index to make.

In PostgreSQL, an update can avoid new entries through a heap-only tuple, or HOT, update when indexed values do not require maintenance and the new version fits on the same table page. Adding an often-changing column to an index can remove that opportunity. Row versions, storage and cleanup [/review/relational-collection/storage/] develops why updates leave old versions and when their space can be reused.

Begin with a query and name the avoided work: scanning unrelated rows, fetching rejected rows, sorting an answer or visiting the table for returned columns. Derive the key and any predicate from that work, check it on representative data, then account for the writes it adds. Live construction and removal have locking and failure behaviour of their own; PostgreSQL schema changes under load [/review/relational-collection/postgresql/schema-changes/] handles that operational step.

r11.text: When an application is slow for one value but a literal query in a console looks fine, compare the actual statement, parameter types and plan mode as well as its text. A representative test includes common values, rare values and large tenants. Changing every prepared statement to custom planning has a cost too. Reading and repairing PostgreSQL plans [/review/relational-collection/postgresql/query-execution/] takes these native diagnostics further.

A distributed measured plan should connect SQL operators to rows and bytes transferred, remote requests, placement and the slowest branch. One hot key or one oversized tenant can give one worker most of the work even when the overall row count is well estimated. CockroachDB query work and hot ranges [/review/relational-collection/cockroachdb/query-performance/] follows its concrete SQL and storage-layer evidence. No multi-machine latency or distributed execution is measured by this article’s local PostgreSQL fixture.

Finally, distinguish slow execution from time spent waiting before or around it. Locks, connection queues and a client consuming rows slowly can dominate a request whose operators are efficient. Diagnosing a database incident [/review/relational-collection/slow-queries/] establishes that boundary. Once execution work is the cause, a useful plan reading should end with a causal statement you can check, rather than a collection of alarming node names.

r12.text: The partition month has a declared time basis. A UTC month and a shop’s local calendar month have different endpoints. As Values, missing data and equality [/review/relational-collection/values/] explains, a named zone’s calendar boundaries must first be interpreted as instants. Writing explicit offsets here keeps connection settings from silently moving the storage boundary.

Pruning does not require an index on the partition key. After excluding partitions, the planner can scan a surviving small piece or use one of its indexes. An endpoint lookup within October might benefit from an endpoint index even though the time bounds performed the pruning. An ID lookup without time bounds might need an index search in every partition. The earlier index article [/review/relational-collection/indexes/] helps choose that route within each surviving piece.

Partition operations also take locks. PostgreSQL’s ordinary detach takes an exclusive parent lock; DETACH … CONCURRENTLY uses a less restrictive parent lock but has additional restrictions and phases, including completion after interruption. It is not a universal “no blocking” switch. Schedule and test the appropriate native operation under the expected readers and writers. Live schema changes and backfills [/review/relational-collection/schema-changes/] develops change protocols under traffic.

The choice of time axis affects the policy. Partitioning by occurrence time lets a late event target an old month. Partitioning by receipt time places it with today’s arrivals, but a retention rule based on occurrence age no longer lines up with whole receipt-time partitions. Keep both timestamps if both questions matter, and say which one owns the storage and expiry boundary. History, correction and deletion [/review/relational-collection/data-lifecycle/] explains why effective and recorded time answer different questions.

Table partitioning here remains inside one PostgreSQL database. Its partitions can all live on the same machine and storage device. It has not created additional independent servers, a replicated copy or a way to keep serving after that machine fails. Splitting a hot current month into named tables also does not automatically split its CPU or disk work across machines. Sharding and distributed SQL [/review/relational-collection/partitioning-and-sharding/] owns those placement and coordination questions.

r13.text: A row constraint is still valuable. It catches negative stock however a writer arrived there. Primary and foreign keys catch duplicate identities and missing parents. Use those constraints alongside the transaction protocol; each closes a different way to reach an invalid state. Constraints and tenant boundaries [/review/relational-collection/constraints/] develops the rules the schema can enforce directly.

Without an explicit transaction, PostgreSQL normally commits each successful statement separately. A successful stock update followed by a failed order insert would then be two separate outcomes. Some drivers manage transactions for you, so check the driver’s behaviour and keep the entire operation on its transaction connection. SQL at the application boundary [/review/relational-collection/application-sql/] follows that boundary into application code.

Keep human input and calls to other services outside this short database transaction. A card provider cannot roll its charge back because PostgreSQL rolled back. A transaction can instead record work to be done later, alongside the order, as Outboxes and database-backed jobs [/review/relational-collection/outboxes-and-jobs/] explains. The separate question of a commit whose reply disappears belongs to Retries when a commit reply is missing [/review/relational-collection/conflicts-and-retries/].

A snapshot determines which committed row versions a read may see. PostgreSQL keeps older versions so an ordinary query can read a consistent view while another transaction changes the rows. It does not have to wait for the writer’s new values. The physical versions and their eventual cleanup are followed in Row versions, storage and cleanup [/review/relational-collection/storage/].

Serializable has a cost. Tracking dependencies takes work, and rejected attempts repeat work; a busy rule can cause many retries. The application needs a bounded retry policy and a way to report that it could not complete. It must also keep irreversible external effects out of attempts that may be discarded. Retries when a commit reply is missing [/review/relational-collection/conflicts-and-retries/] develops retry control and distinguishes a known serialization failure from an uncertain commit reply.

Explicit locking offers another design: make every decision for the same rule coordinate through a common protected row or set of rows. The lock, the time the snapshot is taken and every participating writer must agree. In particular, waiting for a lock does not refresh an existing Repeatable Read snapshot. Locks, contention and deadlocks [/review/relational-collection/locks-and-deadlocks/] works through complete protocols, empty matching sets, waits and lock ordering.

r14.text: The useful scope is the transaction, rather than just the time the select runs. Ending the transaction immediately after reading the stock would release the lock before the purchase used it. A pool helper on another connection would be outside that protection. SQL at the application boundary [/review/relational-collection/application-sql/] follows connection ownership.

Serializable is another complete choice: make all transactions participating in this rule Serializable, keep their reads and writes inside the transaction, and retry serialization failures. Our separate two-reader, two-insert schedule allowed one booking and rejected the other transaction with 40001. Serializable preserves a serial outcome; it does not promise that the first buyer to start wins. Transactions and isolation [/review/relational-collection/transaction-boundaries/] develops that choice.

Keep the guarded transaction short. Do validation that does not depend on changing database state before it starts. Acquire the needed locks, read and change the data, then finish. Waiting for a user, an email provider or another slow service while holding S501 makes everyone behind the holder wait too. External work can be recorded and performed later, as Outboxes and database-backed jobs [/review/relational-collection/outboxes-and-jobs/] explains.

Use that evidence to change the cause: shorten the holder, remove an unnecessary lock, repair ordering or reduce admissions to an overloaded authority. Cancelling a waiting query does not release the holder’s locks. Cancelling the holder’s statement may still leave its transaction needing rollback. Live intervention and detailed PostgreSQL wait tools belong to Operating and diagnosing PostgreSQL [/review/relational-collection/postgresql/operations/].

r15.text: Wide rows use more of each page, so fewer fit in one read. Very large values may be compressed or moved into separate storage; PostgreSQL calls that mechanism TOAST. A large description can then have storage beyond the main table's heap. To understand a table's footprint, count its indexes and any out-of-line values as well as its main file. The PostgreSQL architecture article [/review/relational-collection/postgresql/architecture/] follows those structures in more detail.

Retained row versions are also not an audit trail. Cleanup is allowed to remove them. If the shop must explain which price was believed yesterday and when a correction was recorded, it needs an explicit history model and retention policy, as History, correction and deletion [/review/relational-collection/data-lifecycle/] explains.

Each logical change can consequently produce several physical writes: a new heap version, index changes where needed, and records in the write-ahead log. Later cleanup and file rewrites add more. This excess of physical work over the application change is write amplification. The index article [/review/relational-collection/indexes/] connects it to the set of indexes a query earns; crash recovery [/review/relational-collection/crash-recovery/] follows the log's separate job.

For a busy PostgreSQL service, continue with vacuum and transaction age [/review/relational-collection/postgresql/row-versions/]. Vacuum also maintains visibility information and protects against transaction-ID age problems; treating it only as a way to shrink a file misses jobs the database needs even when disk space looks comfortable.

r16.text: The scratch schema keeps the purchase’s identity, stock, order and lines; historical orders and payments are outside this fixture. Checks compare the complete resulting stock vector and row counts. No provider charge is attempted. Outboxes and database-backed jobs [/review/relational-collection/outboxes-and-jobs/] carries this identity reasoning across a boundary that the database transaction cannot commit for itself.

r17.text: We continue from Retries when a commit reply is missing [/review/relational-collection/conflicts-and-retries/] and Locks, contention and deadlocks [/review/relational-collection/locks-and-deadlocks/]. Order 103 is Mina’s pending purchase of one mug and two packs of tea, worth 29.00. This article adds an outbox event, order-103-created, as an explicitly separate record of intended work. It does not add a payment or claim that an email has been delivered.

r18.text: The two committed histories recover the same purchase. The application knows different things. A crash just before the reply and one just before durable commit can both look like a dropped connection, so the missing reply cannot decide whether Mina should buy again. Retries when a commit reply is missing [/review/relational-collection/conflicts-and-retries/] uses request identity to resolve that uncertainty.

More frequent checkpoints can reduce the log that a restart must replay, while making active pages get written more often. Less frequent checkpoints can reduce repeated page work but leave more recovery work. The useful balance depends on the actual write workload and recovery requirement. PostgreSQL WAL, checkpoints and durability [/review/relational-collection/postgresql/recovery/] develops the settings and the observations that justify changing them.

Crash recovery also faithfully preserves a committed mistake. If an operator deletes order 103 and commits, the log's job is to make that deletion survive. A replica can copy it too. A lost disk or missing recovery files may leave the local log unable to recover anything. Those failures require another usable history, which Backup, restore and reconciliation [/review/relational-collection/backup-and-restore/] follows from a saved copy through acceptance of later valid work.

r19.text: That gate demonstrates the required ordering in one database. A real service may need to revoke application roles, stop other writers, control old credentials and prevent an isolated former primary from resuming writes. Failover and fencing [/review/relational-collection/failover/] develops authority across servers. A gate that only one of several writers obeys is not a closed history.

For an executable operational procedure, continue with Restoring PostgreSQL to a recovery target [/review/relational-collection/postgresql/backup-and-restore/] or CockroachDB backup and recovery [/review/relational-collection/cockroachdb/backup-and-restore/]. Each engine has its own backup dependencies, target semantics and restore commands. Carry the same acceptance question into either: which history is now authoritative, and which valid effects still need to be accounted for?

r20.text: This article follows physical log replication: a primary sends recovery records to a standby, which applies them to its copy of the files. PostgreSQL 18 supplies the concrete terms. Logical replication sends selected data changes instead and has different boundaries; logical replication and change feeds [/review/relational-collection/postgresql/logical-replication/] develops that design.

A replica also reproduces committed mistakes. It is not an earlier clean backup merely because it is on another server. Keep backup and restore [/review/relational-collection/backup-and-restore/] for recovering an earlier history, and continue with failover and fencing [/review/relational-collection/failover/] for transferring write authority to a candidate whose available history you have checked.

r21.text: Some systems coordinate leadership through a separate election or lease service. That authority needs its own failure rules, and the resource being written must enforce the result. An expired lease does not stop a paused process that later resumes unless a check at the relevant boundary rejects its stale authority. The same issue appears in database-backed jobs [/review/relational-collection/outboxes-and-jobs/], where a worker can outlive its lease.

Before accepting writes on a candidate, inspect its log history and progress. A received byte, a durable byte and a replayed change are different observations. Let it apply the usable committed log it has, and compare it with the required boundary when that boundary is known. Replicas, lag and read routing [/review/relational-collection/replicas-and-read-routing/] supplies those progress distinctions.

Resolve uncertain commits as well as acknowledged ones. An in-flight request may have committed on the old side even though the caller never heard success. Preserve identities and compare authoritative outcomes before replaying it. External charges, messages and jobs need their own evidence and compensation decisions, as restore and reconciliation [/review/relational-collection/backup-and-restore/] develops.

Choose failure boundaries honestly. Two local processes demonstrate promotion and conflicting authority. They do not demonstrate independent disks, a regional partition or the reliability of a remote power fence. If the requirement is survival of a machine, rack or region, the placement and control path have to cross that boundary too. Regional placement and survival [/review/relational-collection/regional-placement/] develops those choices.

For PostgreSQL's concrete commands and progress checks, continue with physical replicas and promotion [/review/relational-collection/postgresql/replication/]. The main decision remains the same: before transferring accepted writes, establish who can still write and which history the service is choosing to keep.

r22.text: Existing rows initially have NULL in the new column. Old callers continue naming unit_price. This relies on explicit insert and select column lists. A positional INSERT INTO order_items VALUES (...) or a result unpacked from SELECT * can break on an apparently additive change, as SQL at the application boundary [/review/relational-collection/application-sql/] explains.

PostgreSQL schema changes under load [/review/relational-collection/postgresql/schema-changes/] develops locks, validation scans and index builds. CockroachDB schema jobs under load [/review/relational-collection/cockroachdb/schema-changes/] follows that engine’s asynchronous jobs. Neither engine can infer whether an old application still depends on a column it is asked to remove.

r23.text: We follow the shop’s application, whose requests borrow connections as described in SQL at the application boundary [/review/relational-collection/application-sql/]. The drawings below are deliberately small schedules. Their rounds and limits are invented to make waiting visible; they are not measurements of PostgreSQL or a sizing recommendation.

When the caller gives up, stop work that is no longer useful. Returning an HTTP error while the SQL continues leaves load in the database and can let a retry overlap the original attempt. Cancellation itself has a race with completion. Wait for the driver’s outcome and transaction cleanup; do not return a connection that another task still uses. A missing commit reply also leaves an outcome to resolve, as Retries when a commit reply is missing [/review/relational-collection/conflicts-and-retries/] explains.

Use observations from the same interval. A CPU chart from the morning and a query plan from after the incident do not establish the bottleneck at its peak. Diagnosing a database incident [/review/relational-collection/slow-queries/] develops that investigation; Operating and diagnosing PostgreSQL [/review/relational-collection/postgresql/operations/] follows the engine’s views.

When the evidence points to one hot row, adding servers leaves that rule serial. When it points to independent tenants exceeding one server’s useful capacity, distribution may help, with new coordination and operational costs. Sharding and distributed SQL [/review/relational-collection/partitioning-and-sharding/] develops that choice. First reduce avoidable work, bound what remains and check the recovery state. Those changes give the next capacity decision a stable workload to reason about.

r24.text: Do not turn the query into an automatic “kill every old transaction” rule. An old transaction may be a required operation, and the process ID can later be reused. Before a targeted intervention, recheck the session’s identity, age, current state, affected work and owner. Locks, contention and deadlocks [/review/relational-collection/locks-and-deadlocks/] explains the underlying protocol and the costs of changing it.

Reduce optional traffic or its concurrency while collecting evidence. Give acquisition a bounded wait and refuse excess work in a way clients understand. A fleet-wide restart can make every process reconnect at once, erase useful state and replace one overloaded queue with another. Connections, overload and capacity [/review/relational-collection/connections-and-capacity/] develops the budgets and overload policy after this branch is established.

Compare rows processed with rows returned, estimates with actual counts, repeated loops, pages touched and spills. The detail belongs to Query execution and bad plans [/review/relational-collection/query-execution/]. Avoid declaring a sequential scan wrong just because an index exists. The query may need most of the table, or the index may not match its conditions.

r25.text: The table key makes (10, P7) and (20, P7) distinct. Scoped foreign keys keep stored relationships inside one shop. Neither rule stops a well-formed query from requesting the other shop. Constraints and tenant boundaries [/review/relational-collection/constraints/] separates that integrity question from authorisation.

A proxy or pool can alter that context. If every backend connection runs as an owner while the application merely labels it runtime_10, this policy is not being tested under the intended identity. Verify the effective identity on the actual application connection and test whatever role/context setup the pool performs on checkout. Session settings must not leak to the next borrower; SQL at the application boundary [/review/relational-collection/application-sql/] follows the ownership of that connection and transaction.

Privileged functions, exports, replicas and backups are further paths to the same data. Row policies on ordinary table queries do not establish their authority. Catalogue them separately, including who can call privileged code and who can read copied data. PostgreSQL roles, policies and privileged code [/review/relational-collection/postgresql/access-control/] develops those PostgreSQL-specific boundaries; Operating and securing a CockroachDB cluster [/review/relational-collection/cockroachdb/operations/] follows secure identity and native tenant acceptance there.

r26.text: First establish which pressure you have. Query work, leaked connections or one long transaction can exhaust a server without requiring distribution. Connections, overload and capacity [/review/relational-collection/connections-and-capacity/] supplies the evidence and headroom; Table partitioning and data lifecycle [/review/relational-collection/partitioning/] and Replicas, lag and read routing [/review/relational-collection/replicas-and-read-routing/] develop the other two mechanisms.

A hot single key is different again. Hashing that same key always sends it to the same bucket. Splitting a range can separate different hot keys, but cannot divide one row’s decision among independent owners while preserving its original semantics. Rebalancing and cluster change [/review/relational-collection/rebalancing/] follows the distinction between moving load and removing its source.

The abstraction is valuable because an application can express one transaction without implementing each message. The messages still exist. Replicas must agree about their portion; participants must agree about the transaction; readers need a coherent view. Transactions across partitions [/review/relational-collection/distributed-transactions/] follows the commit boundary, while Time, snapshots and distributed reads [/review/relational-collection/distributed-reads/] follows the read boundary.

r27.text: The isolation protocol remains necessary too. A two-phase commit can faithfully commit two transactions whose decisions violated a business rule at a weaker isolation level. Agreement about a purchase’s outcome does not establish that its stock test was sound. The conditional update and complete transaction logic from Transactions and isolation [/review/relational-collection/transaction-boundaries/] still apply.

Replication can preserve the decision service and let a surviving quorum elect a new authority. The old authority must be unable to produce conflicting accepted decisions. That is the same fencing concern developed in Failover and fencing [/review/relational-collection/failover/]. Making one coordinator highly available reduces its single-process failure risk; it does not let the transaction ignore an unavailable required participant.

CockroachDB, for example, uses write intents and a transaction record, with Parallel Commits rather than exactly the classic message schedule drawn here. The commit condition can be established while later cleanup remains. A provisional value’s presence alone is not proof of a committed transaction. CockroachDB transactions and retries [/review/relational-collection/cockroachdb/transactions/] develops that native protocol.

External card charges and emails are outside the database’s participant set unless they explicitly support and join an appropriate transaction protocol. An outbox can record that work atomically with the purchase, but delivery still needs its own identities and recovery. Outboxes and database-backed jobs [/review/relational-collection/outboxes-and-jobs/] follows that boundary.

Finally, the client can lose its commit reply after the database has decided successfully. Distributed commit does not make that reply infallible. Resolve the same logical request under its stable key before replaying the business action; Retries when a commit reply is missing [/review/relational-collection/conflicts-and-retries/] distinguishes that uncertainty from a known abort.

r28.text: We return to the purchase of order 103, with stock owned by partition A and the order and lines by B. This is the same deliberately split placement used in Transactions across partitions [/review/relational-collection/distributed-transactions/]. The drawings use invented ordered timestamps to explain snapshots; no clock offsets, regional latency or native distributed execution are measured.

“Follower read” also does not universally mean “stale”. Products can provide strong reads from suitable followers under additional protocols and placement choices. CockroachDB distinguishes strong reads for global tables from stale historical follower reads. CockroachDB isolation and follower reads [/review/relational-collection/cockroachdb/follower-reads/] develops the native modes and their restrictions.

The timestamp’s scope also matters for pagination. Choosing “recent enough” independently for each page can let the view change between pages. Reuse an appropriate snapshot identity for the complete export if that is the contract. Pagination and consistent exports [/review/relational-collection/large-results/] follows its lifetime and continuation boundary.

r29.text: Trace the critical dependencies rather than adding every possible regional round trip. A purchase that touches several replica groups also needs its transaction protocol. Some work can overlap; some must wait for an earlier result. Transactions across partitions [/review/relational-collection/distributed-transactions/] separates that decision from the replication of each participant.

Reads have another choice. A nearby replica may serve a certified historical snapshot without contacting the current write authority for every request. That can suit a catalogue whose freshness contract permits it. Mina’s confirmation page must include her successful order, so an older local snapshot may be insufficient. Time, snapshots and distributed reads [/review/relational-collection/distributed-reads/] develops that boundary.

Products package these choices differently. CockroachDB distinguishes regional tables, rows with individual home regions, and global tables aimed at reads across regions. Its database survival goal is a separate setting that affects replication. “Global” is not a promise of cost-free local writes everywhere. The native settings and their interactions belong in CockroachDB table locality and region survival [/review/relational-collection/cockroachdb/locality/].

Inspect actual placement after the database has converged. Include voting and non-voting roles, authorities, secondary indexes and coordination metadata that the product exposes. A desired policy is not evidence that enough healthy replicas have already reached that state. Topology changes have a transfer interval; Rebalancing and cluster change [/review/relational-collection/rebalancing/] follows that work.

r30.text: For the shop, a burst spread across many independent products offers work that can move to different groups. Thousands of buyers competing for the same last P7 mug still need one correct decision about that stock. Splitting a surrounding range does not divide that single row’s entitlement. Sharding and distributed SQL [/review/relational-collection/partitioning-and-sharding/] develops the key and load distinction.

CockroachDB calls these paths draining and decommissioning. Its drain transfers active responsibilities and handles client connections without evacuating all replicas; decommissioning also moves data off the node. Operating and securing a CockroachDB cluster [/review/relational-collection/cockroachdb/operations/] owns the native health checks and removal procedure.

Logical shard movement in a distributed PostgreSQL system has similar boundaries but different mechanisms. It may copy rows and stream changes, then perform a controlled routing cutover. Where distributed PostgreSQL work runs [/review/relational-collection/postgresql/sharding/] owns that implementation. Do not infer a short or lock-free cutover from the word “online”.

Separate installing new binaries from enabling new cluster features or finalising a new format. Products can support a mixed-version interval while retaining an older compatibility mode, then make a later change that narrows or removes rollback options. Keep the exact supported upgrade path and its finalisation boundary with the native procedure; Upgrading a CockroachDB cluster [/review/relational-collection/cockroachdb/upgrades/] develops that case.

r31.text: Backends also share coordination structures, including locks. A long transaction can hold a row lock while doing little CPU work. A page being present in memory therefore says nothing about whether a query can proceed without waiting. Operating and diagnosing PostgreSQL [/review/relational-collection/postgresql/operations/] connects process activity, waits and memory pressure to an incident.

Updates also dirty buffered pages and generate WAL. Background writers and the checkpointer help write data pages; the WAL writer handles another part of the log work. A backend can have to write a dirty buffer itself when it needs to reuse that slot. These processes share the server’s work, but none changes which snapshot may see a tuple. WAL, checkpoints and durability [/review/relational-collection/postgresql/recovery/] follows their ordering and the commit reply.

Finally, obsolete versions need cleanup. HOT chains can be pruned during ordinary page access; vacuum handles broader heap and index maintenance and maintains visibility information. Cleanup cannot discard a version merely because a newer one committed. Vacuum and transaction age [/review/relational-collection/postgresql/row-versions/] follows the boundary that lets old versions go, and the maintenance required even when a table’s visible row count barely changes.

r32.text: Anti-wraparound maintenance can run even when normal autovacuum is disabled. Treat forced activity and age warnings as maintenance urgency, not proof that PostgreSQL will always rescue a neglected cluster. Near exhaustion the server protects data by refusing commands that need new IDs. Use the version’s documented recovery procedure and an operator who can inspect every retention holder. Operating and diagnosing PostgreSQL [/review/relational-collection/postgresql/operations/] owns that intervention.

VACUUM FULL writes a compact replacement and takes an exclusive lock that blocks normal table use. It needs working disk space as well as time. It can solve an established space problem, but it does not make old snapshots cease to exist or supply a sustainable maintenance policy. Index rebuilds and the locks involved belong with schema changes under load [/review/relational-collection/postgresql/schema-changes/].

r33.text: This is a schema illustration, not a claim that the core products table already has those attributes. JSON and structured alternatives [/review/relational-collection/postgresql/json/] develops the representation and checks both predicates natively.

For room reservations, Types and extensions [/review/relational-collection/postgresql/extensions/] combines range semantics with an enforced overlap rule. For geometry, the coordinate system and distance units must be established before an index is meaningful. For embeddings, vector search [/review/relational-collection/postgresql/vector-search/] owns approximate retrieval and its recall test. Sharing an index framework does not make these result contracts interchangeable.

GiST splits and updates depend on its class and data distribution. BRIN’s small summaries can be cheap to maintain but may become less selective. Ordinary indexed values also affect the HOT opportunity described in processes, pages and row versions [/review/relational-collection/postgresql/architecture/]; BRIN’s summarising rule is a specific exception, not evidence that index maintenance is free.

Compare the complete route: operators the class supports, rows or pages it admits, required rechecks, the requested order and visibility checks. Then compare insert and update work with and without the candidate on representative data. Live builds, invalid indexes and safe removal are separate operational steps covered by schema changes under load [/review/relational-collection/postgresql/schema-changes/].

r34.text: First establish whether execution work is actually the delay. A query can wait for a lock, sit behind a connection queue or deliver rows to a slow client. Operator improvements cannot remove an application queue. Operating and diagnosing PostgreSQL [/review/relational-collection/postgresql/operations/] establishes that service boundary.

Keep the general plan-reading rules [/review/relational-collection/query-execution/] in view: a parent can stop its child early, actual rows and times are per-loop averages, and buffer counts already accumulate repeated accesses and child work. They count accesses, not distinct pages. Read from the inputs towards the result, checking each counter’s scope before combining it with another.

r35.text: Use foreign keys for facts that refer to other authoritative rows. A JSON string containing a product code does not become a foreign key merely because the code is well formed. Constraints and tenant boundaries [/review/relational-collection/constraints/] develops that enforcement and why a cross-row lookup inside a check is insufficient.

A JSON-path query can express more complex conditions. Index support depends on the clauses its class can extract; supported operator syntax is not a guarantee that every path predicate is a selective index search. Inspect Index Cond, rechecks and candidate heap work, as index methods and operators [/review/relational-collection/postgresql/indexes/] explains.

During a live transition, decide which representation owns the value and how old and new writers agree. Two independently writable copies invite disagreement. Live schema changes and backfills [/review/relational-collection/schema-changes/] handles the compatible write protocol and final equivalence check.

r36.text: synchronous_commit chooses how much processing a commit waits for before returning success. With no synchronous standbys configured, on, local, remote_write and remote_apply all wait for the local WAL flush. The remote names acquire their additional meaning only when synchronous replication is configured. Physical replicas and promotion [/review/relational-collection/postgresql/replication/] follows those remote boundaries.

Finally, crash recovery preserves the surviving committed history, including mistakes. A durable deletion remains a deletion. Losing the data volume needs a separate usable copy. Restoring PostgreSQL to a recovery target [/review/relational-collection/postgresql/backup-and-restore/] starts from that copy and follows the WAL chain to the intended history; Physical replicas and promotion [/review/relational-collection/postgresql/replication/] asks which remote copy can safely become the writer.

r37.text: A physical standby can shorten the route to another running copy, but it also replays mistakes. Physical replicas and promotion [/review/relational-collection/postgresql/replication/] follows which copy may take authority. Moving the history into a new major version introduces different compatibility and cutover questions, developed in Upgrading and migrating PostgreSQL [/review/relational-collection/postgresql/upgrades/].

r38.text: remote_apply does not refresh a Repeatable Read snapshot established earlier, and a different asynchronous standby can still lag. To read your own write, choose the intended copy, wait for its required history boundary and start a suitable fresh snapshot. Replicas, lag and read routing [/review/relational-collection/replicas-and-read-routing/] develops that application protocol.

First decide who can still write. An unreachable primary may remain alive for another client. Changing DNS or a pool target does not close old sessions. PostgreSQL’s promotion command does not turn off the former primary. Failover and fencing [/review/relational-collection/failover/] explains why an enforced authority boundary must accompany the role change.

Keep application traffic closed until accepted and uncertain requests have been accounted for. If discarded history contains a confirmed purchase, copying only its order row omits its lines and stock effect. External effects have separate authorities too. Recovery and reconciliation [/review/relational-collection/postgresql/backup-and-restore/] follows that complete operation.

r39.text: Where the effect and checkpoint share a transaction authority, commit them together and recognise repeated identities. An external provider action requires its own idempotency or reconciliation protocol. “The slot acknowledged the change” does not establish that an email arrived or a payment happened exactly once. Outboxes and database-backed jobs [/review/relational-collection/outboxes-and-jobs/] develops application intent and delivery separately.

The complete logical-replication drill [/review/relational-collection/evidence/r39/logical-drill.py] exercises initial copying and the identity, schema, sequence and conflicting-write counterexamples on an owned PostgreSQL 18.6 pair. Its controlled final sequence repair stops the source first; it is not a full live migration. Upgrading and migrating PostgreSQL [/review/relational-collection/postgresql/upgrades/] follows cutover, version compatibility and rollback boundaries.

r40.text: We continue the conversion from decimal unit_price to integer unit_price_minor on the shop’s order lines. The integer counts hundredths in this single-unit, fixed-scale example: 20.00 becomes 2000. Live schema changes and backfills [/review/relational-collection/schema-changes/] establishes the compatible caller stages and decimal-authoritative write bridge. Here we carry those stages through PostgreSQL’s locks, validation and index lifecycle. The downloadable drill checks the mechanisms on an owned PostgreSQL 18.6 instance.

Before a retry, inspect the blockers and the stored schema. Retry with a bounded delay and admission limit; an immediate loop can repeatedly put the same exclusive request in front of ordinary traffic. Ending another session is a separate incident decision, developed in Operating and diagnosing PostgreSQL [/review/relational-collection/postgresql/operations/].

The writer population is part of that rule. A privileged import that bypasses the bridge, a disabled trigger or another replication write path needs an explicit contract. The ordinary-write result here does not establish that every possible administrator command preserves it. Roles, policies and privileged code [/review/relational-collection/postgresql/access-control/] follows who can alter those protections.

For a live replacement, accept the intended definition, state and representative query plans before retiring the previous access path. Statistics may need refreshing after a large load or data transformation. A completed build does not prove the planner will choose it, or that the chosen plan saves work; Reading and repairing PostgreSQL plans [/review/relational-collection/postgresql/query-execution/] supplies that comparison.

r41.text: We take the incident method from Diagnosing a database incident [/review/relational-collection/slow-queries/] into a small PostgreSQL 18.6 experiment. Two requests borrow two pooled connections and block on one product row. A third expires before borrowing. We then cancel a waiter and end the identified holder, observing what each action changes. This is a disposable mechanism test, not a production incident or a pool-sizing benchmark.

backend_xmin is a retained transaction horizon when one exists. A long transaction can be relevant to cleanup, but transaction age alone does not tell you which versions it retains. Establish the actual horizon before making a vacuum intervention. Vacuum and transaction age [/review/relational-collection/postgresql/row-versions/] develops that investigation.

Use the monitoring authority appropriate to the task. Ordinary users cannot inspect every other role’s query details. The drill’s owner can inspect its own sessions; that is separate from proving a production monitoring login has the necessary, limited visibility. Roles, policies and privileged code [/review/relational-collection/postgresql/access-control/] separates monitoring, signalling and ownership powers.

pg_blocking_pids includes both conflicting holders and earlier incompatible requests in a lock queue. A prepared transaction can appear as PID 0 because no ordinary live session owns it. Follow the appropriate recovery authority in that case; do not invent a session to terminate. Locks, contention and deadlocks [/review/relational-collection/locks-and-deadlocks/] develops the lock protocol, while Transactions across partitions [/review/relational-collection/distributed-transactions/] explains unresolved prepared work.

That is the recovery cost as well as the improvement: a session and its unfinished transaction were lost. A complete purchase interrupted around commit would need the request-outcome protocol from Retries when a commit reply is missing [/review/relational-collection/conflicts-and-retries/]. Our holder never submitted a commit, and A’s error is a known statement cancellation; the drill does not silently treat an uncertain commit as an abort.

The lock investigation was selected because the activity and ownership evidence supported it. If statements instead reach execution promptly and touch excessive rows, take a representative query and parameter set into Reading and repairing PostgreSQL plans [/review/relational-collection/postgresql/query-execution/]. An estimated plan avoids executing the operation; EXPLAIN ANALYZE runs it and must fit a safe diagnostic scope.

For storage demand, connect the named waits to I/O, WAL and checkpoint evidence over the same interval. For retained versions, establish what holds the cleanup horizon before increasing vacuum work. For planned DDL, inspect its progress and lock budget through Schema changes under load [/review/relational-collection/postgresql/schema-changes/]. A broad maintenance command can add work to a server already short of I/O or free space.

r42.text: We continue the tenant-scoped catalogue from Database access and least privilege [/review/relational-collection/access-control/]. Shop 10 has the Blue mug, P7 at 20.00. Harbour Tea, shop 20, has its own P7, the Copper mug at 18.00. Actual login sessions on a disposable PostgreSQL 18.6 instance will try both permitted work and deliberate escapes. No price change made for a test survives the drill.

r43.text: Logical replication can keep a new destination catching up while the old source serves traffic. That reduces the work left inside the final write pause, but adds a second live system and a stream to operate. Schema, sequences, large objects and other unreplicated state remain separate responsibilities. The physical standby protocol generally does not bridge major versions. Logical replication and change feeds [/review/relational-collection/postgresql/logical-replication/] establishes those boundaries.

r44.text: A non-voting replica keeps another copy but does not count towards a write majority. It can serve eligible follower reads under a historical-read contract. Adding one is different from adding a vote. Isolation and follower reads [/review/relational-collection/cockroachdb/follower-reads/] develops that contract.

Range agreement is also smaller than transaction agreement. A purchase changes stock, an order and its lines, potentially in several ranges. Each range can replicate its work while the transaction is unresolved. The transaction protocol determines whether those changes form a committed purchase. Transactions and retries [/review/relational-collection/cockroachdb/transactions/] follows that additional decision.

Begin with the query and its keys. Identify primary and secondary spans, current leaseholders and voting copies. Then decide whether pressure comes from different keys sharing an interval, a moving index end, a lookup between indexes or contention on one row. Query work and hot ranges [/review/relational-collection/cockroachdb/query-performance/] develops remedies; Table locality and region survival [/review/relational-collection/cockroachdb/locality/] adds geographic placement.

r45.text: Record an outbox event with the order if downstream work must follow the purchase. Delivery then has its own identity and recovery contract. The database’s purchase key does not automatically deduplicate a payment provider. Outboxes and database-backed jobs [/review/relational-collection/outboxes-and-jobs/] develops that boundary.

The forced error and withheld acknowledgement are explicit injections. No native 40003, network partition, provider effect or production driver’s automatic replay is claimed. These tests establish the chosen application protocol; they do not measure a distributed commit’s messages or geographic latency. Isolation and follower reads [/review/relational-collection/cockroachdb/follower-reads/] next separates authoritative decisions from eligible historical observations.

r46.text: Plan the maximum lifetime of a report, its restart behaviour and the versions that must remain available. Choosing a relative timestamp independently for each page creates a moving view; retaining one exact timestamp creates a lifetime requirement. Pagination and consistent exports [/review/relational-collection/large-results/] develops that continuation contract.

Strong follower reads for GLOBAL tables are another placement contract. They should not be confused with deliberately stale reads. Table locality and region survival [/review/relational-collection/cockroachdb/locality/] develops that choice and its write cost.

r47.text: Transactions and retries [/review/relational-collection/cockroachdb/transactions/] owns the purchase protocol under contention. Table locality and region survival [/review/relational-collection/cockroachdb/locality/] adds placement and regional communication costs. Keep those contracts while reducing the work each operation needs.

r48.text: The distinction matters during repair and topology change. A database can have the right desired constraints and temporarily lack enough replicas in the required places. A plan can also reveal an unexpected remote lookup despite suitable table homes. Query work and hot ranges [/review/relational-collection/cockroachdb/query-performance/] develops that execution check.

Record the actual versions, topology, operation and load with the results. Verify restored redundancy and headroom as well as the first successful request. Operating a CockroachDB cluster [/review/relational-collection/cockroachdb/operations/] develops the operational response; transactions and retries [/review/relational-collection/cockroachdb/transactions/] supplies the purchase outcome contract.

r49.text: Table privileges alone do not separate the two shops. A runtime with SELECT on the tenant product table can ask for both P7 rows unless another rule restricts rows. A composite primary key prevents the rows being confused as identities; it does not authorise the caller. This is the same distinction established in Database access and least privilege [/review/relational-collection/access-control/].

The connection and permission tests above can be used on their own. Node maintenance needs a further model: Keys, ranges and replication [/review/relational-collection/cockroachdb/keys-and-ranges/] follows SQL data into ranges, their voting copies and the leaseholder that coordinates ordinary access. Then Rebalancing and cluster change [/review/relational-collection/rebalancing/] follows copying, catch-up and safe membership changes, including the capacity and failure allowance needed while data moves. Use that preparation before the health checks and permanent removal below.

Do not fix every replication alarm by reducing the configured replica count. That can silence a mismatch by reducing the promise. Restore eligible capacity or connectivity, then verify that the intended placement has returned. Locality labels describe the configured topology; they do not prove separate power, storage or network failures. Table locality and region survival [/review/relational-collection/cockroachdb/locality/] develops that larger placement contract.

For the next maintenance operation, Upgrading a CockroachDB cluster [/review/relational-collection/cockroachdb/upgrades/] adds binary and cluster-version boundaries. Backup and recovery [/review/relational-collection/cockroachdb/backup-and-restore/] handles the saved history that replication cannot provide after a valid but mistaken write.

r50.text: Before the final enumeration, fence every old write path, resolve previously admitted transactions and look up uncertain request outcomes. Keep that history closed through reconciliation and acceptance. Backup, restore and reconciliation [/review/relational-collection/backup-and-restore/] develops the general authority contract; CockroachDB's backup does not enforce it for the application.

A return to the old source is a new authority transfer once the candidate accepts writes. Those newer operations must be reconciled too. Keep the old source fenced until such a procedure has closed and accounted for the new history; changing a connection address back is not a recovery plan. Moving a SQL application to CockroachDB [/review/relational-collection/cockroachdb/migration/] applies that same boundary to an engine migration.

r51.text: Live schema changes and backfills [/review/relational-collection/schema-changes/] establishes the application protocol: expand compatibly, keep new writes correct, fill existing rows, accept the new representation, then retire old callers before removing their interface. Online schema machinery handles database transitions; it cannot retire a forgotten worker or make yesterday's application understand a new unit.

The native fixture stops after accepting derived integer reads and enforcing the scratch unique key. It does not perform an integer-only writer handover, remove the decimal, measure production load or simulate independent machines. Upgrading a CockroachDB cluster [/review/relational-collection/cockroachdb/upgrades/] owns the different compatibility boundary between binaries and cluster version.

r52.text: Keep a tested recovery route alongside the rollout. A backup must be restorable with the chosen version and scope; its mere existence does not prove a way back. CockroachDB backup and recovery [/review/relational-collection/cockroachdb/backup-and-restore/] develops the saved chain and reconciliation of valid work that a restore excludes.

r53.text: Check transaction behaviour separately. PostgreSQL normally defaults to Read Committed; CockroachDB normally defaults to Serializable and can require whole-transaction retries with SQLSTATE 40001. Choose the target isolation deliberately and preserve the business rule under that protocol. A transport failure during commit still leaves an uncertain outcome, not an instruction to invent another purchase key. Retries when a commit reply is missing [/review/relational-collection/conflicts-and-retries/] develops that distinction.

Re-establish and test roles, ownership, runtime grants, policies, TLS identities and connection routes in the target deployment too. A successful copy run as administrator cannot prove that the application can use its rows or that an unrelated caller cannot. Operating and securing a CockroachDB cluster [/review/relational-collection/cockroachdb/operations/] develops those checks.

The fixture creates no provider payments, messages or emails. A real return must reconcile those authorities too: a missing outbox row on PostgreSQL cannot prove that CockroachDB's worker never sent its event. Preserve effect identities and consult the provider or consumer's record before repeating external work. CockroachDB backup and recovery [/review/relational-collection/cockroachdb/backup-and-restore/] develops the same problem when replacement history comes from a restore.

r54.text: A native PostgreSQL partition is a table belonging to a partitioned relation. Partition pruning can avoid irrelevant pieces, and old pieces can be detached as part of a retention policy. Ordinary local partitions still belong to the same database instance. Splitting a table into those pieces does not create independent PostgreSQL servers, a routing service or a failover protocol. The partitioning article [/review/relational-collection/partitioning/] follows that lifecycle.

Now expose both catalogues through a UNION ALL view and ask for every P7. This appends compatible rows from the two catalogues, preserving each contribution rather than matching pairs or removing duplicates. The shop ID keeps Blue mug and Copper mug distinct. Joins and the meaning of a result row [/review/relational-collection/query-results/#appending-results] works through that result-combination rule.

This is a read-boundary result. It is not an experiment in distributed commit. PostgreSQL 18’s postgres_fdw does not support preparing its remote transactions for two-phase commit. If a workflow must atomically change several databases and recover a decision after a participant failure, choose and verify a protocol that provides that property. A transaction-shaped interface is insufficient evidence; transactions across partitions [/review/relational-collection/distributed-transactions/] develops the required decision and recovery state.

Citus supplies its own online rebalancing operations and co-location rules; use those supported operations for Citus-managed shards. Adding a worker alone does not relocate existing shards. Movement consumes copying, replication and coordination capacity, so test it under the workload it is meant to relieve. The rebalancing article [/review/relational-collection/rebalancing/] follows the general membership and movement problem.

r55.text: The product identifier breaks ties within one query. It does not freeze a multi-page search while documents or stock change. If a long export requires stable membership and ordering, use the appropriate snapshot and pagination boundary [/review/relational-collection/large-results/].

Some intents belong in structured data. If an application needs a product-type filter, model and maintain that fact rather than inferring it from every sentence containing “mug”. Other intents may benefit from curated synonyms, spelling support or vector retrieval [/review/relational-collection/postgresql/vector-search/]. Each changes the candidates or their ordering and needs its own evaluation; changing the representation is not evidence of improvement.

r56.text: The pgvector extension adds vector types, distance operators and nearest-neighbour index methods to PostgreSQL. This article’s native drill runs PostgreSQL 18.6 with pgvector 0.8.7. The extension must be available on the server before CREATE EXTENSION vector can enable it in a database; extension lifecycle [/review/relational-collection/postgresql/extensions/] covers that operational boundary.

A hybrid search can combine lexical candidates [/review/relational-collection/postgresql/full-text-search/] with vector candidates, but their raw scores are not automatically comparable. A fusion or reranking rule needs its own evaluation. Reranking can improve the ordering of candidates already found; it cannot rescue a relevant item omitted by every candidate source.

r57.text: Built-in range types need no extension. tstzrange uses timestamp-with-time-zone instants; tsrange uses zone-free calendar readings. Use the former when reservations occupy particular instants. The display zone remains a separate concern, as Values, missing data and equality [/review/relational-collection/values/] explains.

Use the supported package and PostgreSQL-major-version combination. Installing into a schema does not give that schema an isolated execution engine: extension functions still run in the database server’s processes, and native code can have the server process’s capabilities. Keep installation schemas and search paths controlled. Roles, policies and privileged code [/review/relational-collection/postgresql/access-control/] handles that authority boundary.

Keep that path separate from a PostgreSQL major upgrade. The target server needs compatible extension libraries, and the extension may impose an ordering on its own update. Upgrading and migrating PostgreSQL [/review/relational-collection/postgresql/upgrades/] owns the server route. A backup is useful only if the older environment and a supported recovery path remain available when needed.

assessment.method: Complete finished source and destination readings plus each advertised handoff; route reachability is an inventory, not a teaching verdict.
